subtopic: PROPOSED REFERENCE TO SUPREME COURT OF QUESTION OF LEGISLATIVE POWERS
speechtext:
On the 19th instant, as reported on
page 2216 of Hansard, I asked the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) a question in regard to a resolution standing in my name respecting orientals. In reply to the last part of my question he said that the Minister of Justice would take the matter into consideration. Would the Minister of Justice say whether he has reached any decision?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: PROPOSED REFERENCE TO SUPREME COURT OF QUESTION OF LEGISLATIVE POWERS
speechtext: The matter referred to in the resolution of my hon. friend was also submitted to the department by the hon. member for Comox-Alberni (Mr. Neill) some time ago. The trouble is the resolution seems to ask that certain questions which are of rather an academic character should be referred for decision to the Supreme Court of Canada, and our experience is that the court usually declines to answer such questions. There is no doubt that matters which for all purposes relate to aliens come under the exclusive jurisdiction of the parliament of Canada. The difficulty is that with respect to certain questions it is not always easy to ascertain whether the essence of the question comes within the meaning of the word " alien " under the British North America Act. If my hon. friend has in mind any special statute or regulation the validity of which he would like to be submitted to the supreme court, I shall be very pleased to have the Department of Justice look into the matter; but again, I repeat, questions of a general character I would not like to submit to the supreme court.

Hon. CHARLES A. DUNNING (Minister of Finance):	My hon. friend from Lincoln (Mr. Chaplin) last night raised a question relating to item 94 and item 105, which were left standing. I intimated that in the

Ways and Means-Customs Tariff
meantime I would look into the question he raised. I now desire to suggest, in order that there may be no doubt either as to definitions or otherwise, that item 105 be amended by inserting the words "crushed or" immediately before the word "frozen." The item would then read:	Fruit pulp, with sugar or not,
n.o.p., and fruits crushed or frozen, per pound. That leaves no doubt as to the inclusion of crushed fruits in that item. Is that satisfactory to my hon. friend?

The change as far as I am concerned is satisfactory, but I want to say this to the minister. When you have an article like grapes bearing only a two cents a pound duty, and you put the other item of crushed grapes in at three cents a pound, you are giving more protection than the growers ask for. It makes the thing look more or less ridiculous. That is one feature of it. A duty of three cents a pound on fruit pulp may be reasonable, but on crushed grapes it is not reasonable. That is the difference.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I have no desire to include it in an item which carries a higher rate of duty, but there has been consulation, from the point of view of administration, with the customs department, and they say that it ought to be administered under this fruit pulp item. I shall not enter into a debate on the matter. I prefer very much to have it in the other item, but for administration purposes they say that this is the place.

I shall have to abide by
the advice of the administrators, but it seems to me that the minister himself is responsible, and not the officials who are administering the tariff. The most that the growers of this article ask for is two cents a pound. They do not want any more. To give a higher duty makes it look ridiculous. It is not needed However, if the minister has made up his mind, I am prepared to let the matter go. I want, however, to discuss the matter of grape juice, which is far more important to me, because aa I pointed out yesterday the duty on the crushed grapes is two cents a pound. On that same basis there should be a higher duty on grape juice; otherwise, you might as well cut out the other duty. This morning I received a dozen telegrams from growers in different parts of my county. I will read one. It is from the Niagara Packers, Limited:
Respecting tariff amendments, we respectfully beg to request that a duty of twenty-five cents a gallon be placed on the importation of grape juice tested not over ten degrees Baume test, and a further two and one-half cents a gallon on each additional degree.
That is for the concentrated grape juice. In my remarks yesterday with respect to this matter, I pointed out to the minister that the tariff board had considered this article, and the minister was rather annoyed and said that the matter had not been discussed by the tariff board. Now, on page 33 of the fruits and vegetables report the tariff board set out a schedule. They do not promise any change of duties, they simply publish last year's duties. But here is the schedule, which confirms my contention:
Proposed item:
(a)	Grapes in their natural state or crushed when imported from a country which imposes a customs duty on fruit produced in Canada, weight of package to be included in weight for duty, per pound: British preferential tariff. 1J cents; intermediate tariff, If cents; general tariff, 2 cents.
(b)	Grapes in their natural state or crushed,
per pound:	British preferential tariff, free;
intermediate tariff, If cents; general tariff, 2 cents.
(c)	Grape juice, per gallon wine measure, 25 cents.
The matter was thoroughly discussed by the fruit growers. I admit that afterwards it was learned that concentrated grape juice could be brought in, and they proposed that that should be taken care of in the way I have mentioned. If grape juice comes in concentrated, and if, for instance, five gallons can be concentrated into one, then that one gallon of concentrated juice should carry the same duty as the original five gallons would have carried. I have half a dozen telegrams from the grape growers of my constituency. Here is one from Vineland which is in the western part:
The members of our association representing a very large percentage of the grape growing industry are very much disturbed by reported omission of grape juice and grape juice concentrates. The lack of protection on. this item for even the year nineteen thirty would by reason of the nature of this product prove disastrous to the grape growing industry.
That is signed by C. W. Bauer, president. Here is another from one of the largest wineries in Canada. They make fifty-five per cent of all the wine made in Ontario. This telegram comes from the adjoining riding:
The agent for the California Grape Growers Association here Monday soliciting orders for concentrated grape juice. Advised they expect to ship one million gallons concentrate to Canada this year which would produce more wine than made from Canadian grapes in one year. California surplus grapes in former years produced an over supply of raisins and Sherman Act did not allow fruit being destroyed so this year the California grape growers assisted by the federal farm board are making plans to take care of surplus grapes by using them for concentrated juice which will be sold for any-

Ways and Means-Customs Tariff
thing to get rid of it. The federal farm board have already advanced thirty million dollars to the Cooperative Grape Growers Association to save the grape growing industry in the United States. Surely the Canadian growers will receive some protection against this.
These people know what the importation of this concentrated grape juice would mean. The grape growers, those who produce the grapes, represent the primary industry. I do not care a snap of the fingers for the wineries themselves. I want to look after the people who produce the grapes; I am interested in them. Some of these wineries wanted less duty imposed. They are friends of mine, but I had nerve enough to tell them that they were wrong, that they should not ask such a thing, that they would be killing an industry of the country, something that is rooted in the soil.

Mr. Chairman, I also
have received a number of telegrams with regard to this matter. If the minister had said, " I am in possession of all this information, I have decided upon a definite course, and that course I am going to take;" I would have had nothing further to say, because it would be futile. But this is an important industry and we should encourage it. Heretofore growing grapes has not been a very-I emphasize the " very '-large industry in our country. Now there is an opportunity for it to develop and every class in the community should encourage it. I think some of these people have a real grievance. 1 cannot guarantee that they have because I do not know enough about the case, but I have learned sufficient to make me desire to know more about it. I think it would be in the interests of the country generally if the minister would take a few moments to consult with his experts. Then he could tell us, " I have said'all I intend to Say on this matter;" or, " I do realize that the case of the grape growing industry should be further considered." I have received the following telegram from Beamsville:
Our association who have been urging for months past that full necessary protection be given their product against grapes and grape juice plain and concentrated imported from United States or elsewhere are shocked to learn that there is grave danger of the item covering grape juice being left out of the budget. The effect of this upon our industry will be calamitous even if we are without protection for this year alone. We would again emphasize our request that provision be made in present budget for duty on grape juice effective for coming season's crop.
As I understand the situation, the California grape growers cannot gelt rid of their fruit and are rendering it down-shall I call it?-and

shipping it over here just to get rid of it at any price. It cannot be the minister's idea, and I am sure it is not the opinion of this house, that a staple industry should be subject to any such competition. Neither free trade, high protection nor low protection enters into it. So I ask pleadingly that the minister should consider this matter. Then, if he says, "I have nothing further to say about it;" I shall accept his answer. I do think further consideration ought to be given to this important industry.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, as I indicated yesterday, there appeared, so far as the evidence before the tariff advisory board went, to be a new problem last year land the year before, represented by the crushed grapes to which my hon. friend from Lincoln refers. The crushed grapes are provided for in the item of fruit pulp which I proposed, and certainly they are definitely provided for by the amendment which I have to-day proposed for the purpose of clarification. Concentrated grape juice has not yet come into Canada, and it only arose as a possible factor a short time ago since the matter was inquired into. I have received, even from those interested, varying kinds of advice as to how the situation should be dealt with. Undoubtedly as the tariff now stands, concentrated grape juice is on an ad valorem basis, that is, it would bear a duty of 22i per cent. The first request of the grape growers, before they knew of the existence of concentrated grape juice, was for a duty of 26 cents per gallon specific on grape juice instead of 22J per cent ad valorem. Of course, since they have learned of the posibility of concentrated grape juice coming in, they realize that their request of 26 cents per gallon would be only 6 cents per gallon on the concentrated article, and they would be worse off with regard to concentrated grape juice than they were under the ad valorem tariff of 22J per cent. My reason, quite frankly, for not proposing something of a definite character with respect to concentrated grape juice is that we have not yet got all the facts upon which we can base intelligent action. I will say to my hon. friend from East Toronto (Mr. Ryckman), who spoke very reasonably a moment ago in connection with the matter, that grape juice is not included in the present tariff proposals. It would not affect either of the items which have been left standing, in any case. I shall endeavour to stimulate all the inquiry I can between now and the time these tariff resolutions are disposed of with a view, if possible, to proposing something which will deal with

Ways and Means-Customs Tariff
a matter which up to now has been an hypothetical situation with respect to grape juice. I do not make any definite promise, however, as to accomplishing very much.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: What would concentrates pay if they came in now?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: They would pay 22i per cent ad valorem. If we leave things alone altogether they will continue to pay that amount. We have no information at all as to values. It is suggested that we might adjust the matter by using the Baume gravity test and other technical means of that nature. It is .very easy to make a mistake in jumping at a matter of this sort.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: We have already learned that.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: It is a matter which is very technical in character and it only arose a very few weeks ago. I am not in a position to say more at the moment.

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext:
Amendment agreed to.
Item as amended agreed to.
Customs tariff-94. Grapes, fresh, in their natural state, the weight of the packages to be included iu the weight for duty, per pound: British preferential tariff, free; intermediate tariff, H cents; general tariff, 2 cents.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: That is standing, and is carried by reason of this amendment.

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext:
Item agreed to.
Customs tariff-109. Nuts of all kinds, n.o.p., including shelled peanuts, n.o.p., per pound: British preferential tariff, 1 cent; intermediate tariff, 2 cents; general tariff, 2 cents.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: Is item 106 passed?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Yes. There is no change in item 109.

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext:
Item agreed to.
Customs tariff-109(a). Peanuts, green, in tlie shell or not further processed than shelled: British preferential tariff, free; intermediate tariff, 1 cent; general tariff, 1 cent.
How much of our peanut importation is affected by the change which has been made?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
I will give the reason for the reduction in duty. It will be noticed that whereas formerly all nuts came in under item 109 at 1 cent, 2 cents and 2 cents respectively, it is now proposed to add an item for green peanuts in the shell or not further processed than shelled. The rates applying to this section are, under the British preferential tariff, free; under the intermediate tariff, 1 cent; and under the general tariff, 1 cent.
The reason is that the people concerned have appeared before the tariff board on several occasions. This year the duty on raw shelled peanuts amounts to over 50 per cent ad valorem on the cost of freight value at Vancouver. That is the way the duty works out at the present time on shelled peanuts. In answer to the question of my hon. friend I say the net result is a reduction of all duties on green peanuts in the shell and raw shelled peanuts. The imports in 1929 were valued at $481,000, of which sum $309,000 worth came from China. The imports of raw shelled peanuts are included in the gross total of shelled peanuts which entered the country to a value of $1,174,000 of which $738,000 worth came from the United States.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: They will now come in at 100 per cent less duty from the United States.

speakerposition: Minister of National Revenue
speechtext: No, 100 per cent less duty would wipe it out altogether.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: I meant to say that they would come in at half the duty.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: The peanuts which are being allowed in cheaper are peanuts which are used generally in the manufacture of foods of various kinds and which are mixed with foods and cakes and things of that nature. In that connection it was represented to the tariff board that 50 per cent duty on goods of that kind which were being used largely for food purposes was entirely too high.

What proportion of our
imports is affected? What proportion will come in free, or what amount?

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: There would seem to be very little. The figures given would indicate that practically nothing would come in from the British Empire.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: We have nothing of any consequence from the British Empire at the present time; it is a Chinese and United States product.
I understood that.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: It runs in my mind that there was some discussion about an African treaty, but I am not certain about it. Peanuts may be one of the commodities which are not produced within the British Empire; I would not like to speak with any degree of certainty in connection with that.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext:
I think they are produced.

Ways and Means-Customs Tariff
I learn from what the minister has stated that the amount of duty paid on the importation of peanuts would not be materially affected. May I take that meaning?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I would not say that.

I gathered that peanuts
would come in at the present time practically the same as they had come in before, and the fact of putting them on the free list would not affect the duty which would have to be paid on the peanuts.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: No. My hon. friend forgets that green peanuts in the shell or not further processed than shelled, which are the classes of peanuts used in the food industries throughout Canada, will be reduced under the general tariff from 2 cents to 1 cent per pound.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext:
This is really a peanut
policy.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: They have been applying for it for years.

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext:
Item agreed to.
Customs tariff-135 (a). Invert sugar and all solutions of sugar or invert sugar and water which cannot be completely tested by the polari-scope, not including syrups in receptacles not greater than 60 pounds in gross weight:
When exceeding 56 per centum but not exceeding 65 per centum total sugars, per 100 pounds: British preferential tariff, 68 cents; intermediate tariff, $1.23; general tariff, $1.23.
When exceeding 65 per centum but not exceeding 70 per centum total sugars, per 100 pounds: British preferential tariff, 74 cents; intermediate tariff, $1.33; general tariff, $1.33.
When exceeding 70 per centum total sugars, per 100 pounds: British preferential tariff, 83 cents; intermediate tariff, $1.50; general tariff, $1.50.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
In connection 'with this
item two points were raised during the budget debate. There was a feeling that this involved an increase in the duty on sugar and that it involved an increase in the duty on table syrup. I wish to say to members of the committee that it does neither. It is merely a means of overcoming what is now recognized to be an evasion of the duties on sugar. The proposal here is merely to make sure that this invert sugar, which is really sugar in liquid form, will be taxable at the same rate as sugar. The item will not affect table syrups, nor will it affect sugar; it has nothing to do with either of those items. The government chemists made some suggestions with regard to the technical terms and I propose that we should amend the item, so far as the lMr. Bennett.]
technical terms are concerned, in accordance with the draft which you have before you. It is merely a matter of including terms which are nominally correct for analytical purposes.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: How will it read?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
The amendment will be as follows:
Invert sugar and syrups, a product of the sugar cane or beet, and all imitations thereof or substitutes therefor, not including molasses and not including syrups in receptacles of such size that the gross weight of receptacle and contents does not exceed 60 pounds:
When the total of reducing sugars after inversion is equivalent to more than 56 per cent, but not more than 65 per cent of invert sugars, per 100 pounds: British preferential tariff, 68 cents; intermediate tariff, $1.23; general tariff, $1.23.
When the total of reducing sugars after in-^rsion is equivalent to more than 65 per cent but not more than 70 per cent of invert sugar, per 100 pounds: British preferential tariff, 74 cents; intermediate tariff, $1.33; general tariff, $1.33.
When the total of reducing sugars after inversion is equivalent to more than 70 per cent of invert sugar, per 100 pounds: British preferential tariff, 83 cents; intermediate tariff, $1.50; general tariff, $1.50.
My hon. friend will see that it is just a matter of technical terms.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext:
Except you have added
"not including molasses."

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
Yes, to make sure that
nothing of that character is included.
What is the duty on raw sugar at the present time?

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext:
It depends on certain
[DOT]technical tests.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: It corresponds to these,, technically. The present sugar duties take up-two pages of the customs tariff, and they are based upon the degrees of polarization, per hundred pounds. My hon. friend does not want me to read two whole pages, I am sure, but he can find them on pages 27 and 28 of schedule A of the customs tariff.

What industries use this
invert sugar?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
Canning, to some extent; confectionery, to some extent; jam making, to some extent; any industry which can use liquid sugar. It is rather technical, because there are some industries which require the sugar in actual syrup form, to whom invert sugar properly so described would not be of use.

Ways and Means-Customs Tariff
Has the minister the amount of this invert sugar which was imported into this country last year?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: The import of it in this form, as distinct from the syrups which of course come in legitimately at a low duty, started not more than a couple of years ago. Last year the evidence before the tariff board indicated that some three hundred railway tank cars, came in.

Will the minister say if
there is any difficulty in distinguishing between syrup and invert sugar?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
None at all, by the
technical test which is here imposed It has been submitted to the chemist for that purpose.

Is there anything in this
item which will be of assistance to plants making starch and corn syrup? Is there anything in this item which will assist them in any way?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
That is difficult to say;
the two things really are not interchangeable. In order to make absolutely sure that there would be no difference in the syrup aspect of this, we made clear that not only we excepted molasses but that we did not include syrup of any kind in receptacles of less than sixty pounds in weight.

The reason I am asking
is that there are a number of plants, or one at least, in Canada which are idle but which did make starch and corn syrup. I was wondering if this would assist them in opening; I was hoping it would.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: There is a possibility that by conversion to a limited degree the making of invert sugar might be carried on in such plants which are established on the basis of corn syrup production. My hon. friend can understand how highly technical the whole matter is, and I do not want to be too positive. I can say, however, that under the investigation by the tariff board it was well recognized by everyone that so far as the invert sugar was concerned, the new method of dealing with it by importing it in tank cars represented an evasion of the statutes with respect to the duties on sugar.

The old duty on this was
50 cents; now it is raised to $1.23 and the minister says that makes no difference.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
No, not in syrup. My
hon. friend will understand that by inverting the sugar, by liquefying the sugar, it qualified under the old syrup item instead of coming in
as sugar. That is why the figures shown opposite the tariff item are the syrup figures. It evaded the sugar duty and came in under the lower rate.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: And you are now putting it on the sugar basis?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: We are now putting it on the sugar basis.
Then the 50 cent basis does not apply to invert sugar?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: No.
There is nothing in this item which would increase the trade with the British Empire?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Well, there is a possibility, of course, to the extent that our own refiners get their sugar from the West Indies, principally. This invert sugar comes in of course from the United States, as my hon. friend understands, and in that case it is principally Cuban or Porto Rican sugar, which displaces Canadian sugar.
Could the minister tell us whether there was any invert sugar made in Canada last year?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: In consequence of this importation last year it was made experimentally for the first time. It is likely to be made commercially in the not distant future to deal with this class of trade which really needs liquid sugar as such.

On the face of it this looks like an increase in protection afforded to anyone who wants to make invert sugar. Of course, I understand the minister's statement to be exactly to the contrary, but that is how it looks by reading the tariff item. If the minister will positively assure the house that there is no difference in the amount of duty to be charged, based on whatever test he is using here, there could be no objection to it.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I can illustrate it very simply to my hon. friend by telling him that these importations last year went as high as 70 per cent of solid sugar, and yet they were coming in as table syrup. He will understand that is manifestly a complete subversion of the use of our tariff. If we have a duty on sugar we must apply the duty to sugar, but by the process of inversion it was possible to get by technically as syrup, which really it is not at all.

It is really a thick syrup?

Ways ana Means-Customs Tariff

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: It was really sugar held in solution; that would be a more accurate description.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: No, sugar held in suspension, and it settled and the sugar was available as such.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Yes, that is correct.

It would help us to understand the item if the minister could tell us what the percentage of sugar may be in a heavy sugar syrup. I have not the faintest idea what it may be, but it is possible that it might be 50 per cent.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I cannot answer that offhand, but my hon. friend will notice that I have protected it in the item-at least I have not protected it-I have carefully avoided the possibility of genuine syrup being affected by including in the item the provision that it shall not include molasses or syrups in receptacles of such size that the gross weight of the receptacle and the contents does not exceed 60 pounds. That is to say, if they want to bring in invert sugar as syrup in receptacles of less than 60 pounds, even yet they can get away with that, but as a matter of fact it is known that it would be uneconomical to handle it in that fashion. It is a tank car proposition.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: Should not they be able to bring in syrup in tank cars, glass lined?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: We are advised that there is no demand anywhere for that method of transporting syrup. My hon. friend will understand that invert sugars are easier to handle than syrup.
We did not have the minister's amendment before us; we only heard it read, and it was rather lengthy and we could not grasp everything that was in it.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: If it is desired I will gladly read it again, but I can assure my hon. friend that it is a chemist's description of the test to be applied and is exactly the same in its practical effect as the original wording. There is no difference otherwise at all, and I am sure the technical terms used would mean no more to my hon. friend than they do to me, in actual fact.

Glucose or grape sugar, glucose syrup and corn syrup, or any syrups containing an admixture thereof

That item does not appear on this sheet.

Has the minister considered
giving Great Britain some preference on these items?

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext:
The apple growers of
British Columbia and of Nova Scotia have been endeavouring to produce a cider of a quality comparable to British cider. The little protection which they had permitted a foundation to be laid for this industry, but that small measure of protection is being removed. The hon. gentleman knows that a great effort has been made in recent years to extend the sale in Canada of British cider and since prohibition has been in force, this drink has had a very considerable vogue.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
All cider would not
qualify for prohibition uses; I am thinking of the old Somerset cider.

Ways and Means-Customs Tariff

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext:
I was thinking of the
cider sold by Bulmer's and other manufacturers. I was informed last year that a very considerable sum of money had been expended in taking care of the industry in British Columbia, where considerable quantities of apples have decayed because there was no market for them. The same situation exists in Ontario. The effect of this item will be to deprive this industry of the little protection it had in the past. Cider from Great Britain will be on the free list, whereas previously it paid a duty of 10 cents per gallon for the clarified, and 5 cents a gallon for the unrefined. I think this matter is worthy of serious consideration. The loss of apples due to conditions which have been referred to already is tremendous, and it is very essential that this industry should be stimulated. I had no idea of the magnitude of this industry in England until I had occasion to investigate it because of an endeavour being made by some friends to establish themselves in British Columbia, Nova Scotia and Ontario. The dining cars now sell a brand of cider known as Evangeline, which is made from Nova Scotia apples. This is a cider mixed with soda, and considerable trade has been developed. Tremendous efforts have been made to extend the cider business of Great Britain into the overseas countries, and I feel quite certain that the passage of this item will be very injurious to the endeavours being made to establish such an industry in Canada.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I appreciate the manner in which my hon. friend has approached this question. In investigating this particular commodity, I was somewhat surprised to find that there were no imports from Great Britain of both items, and the total imports from other countries of the first item were valued at only $7, and of the second item, at $240, of which $118 worth came from Switzerland. I cannot comprehend why there were imports from Switzerland.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext:
I think I can help the
minister out on that; I believe those importations were for the purpose of experimentation in connection with the establishment of the industry. I happen to know what has been going on in that direction, and there are some gentlemen who are very earnestly endeavouring to establish this business in British Columbia. The fact is that the existing duty has been prohibitive so far as cider is concerned- perhaps not prohibitive, but it has been sufficient.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
My hon. friend is quite
right, it was prohibitive.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: My hon. friend probably knows of the advertisements which appear quite frequently in Punch with respect to a very well known brand of British cider, known practically the world over. Up to the present time, that cider has not entered the Canadian market, but I think the elimination of the protection at present in force will destroy any possibility of our developing the industry in this country''.

In view of the fact that the importation of cider has been almost nil, why has the tariff been changed? Does the minister want to kill the industry we have built up in this country? A considerable business has been built up in my constituency, particularly in the Evangeline cider referred to by my hon. leader. Now the minister is going to open it up, and make cider free from all countries.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: No.
If there have been no importations, why has this item been touched? Is it just to increase the list of free items from British countries?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: My hon. friend has made two incorrect statements. He said that it is proposed to make cider free from all countries; that is the first error. My hon. friend stated that this item has been included merely to increase the list with regard to-
I meant from all British countries.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: My observation has been that cider is not a drink commonly in use in Canada.
There is a great deal of it used.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I believe the production of cider is confined at the present time to the Evangeline plant. My information is that the degree of protection has nothing to do with this commodity, the situation is rather one of economy in production and up to the present time Canada has not been able to develop that economy. I thought that if a reasonable opportunity were given to Canadian people to drink British cider-

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext:
What about allowing
them to drink Canadian cider?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
-that would not injure the Canadian cider industry. From the information I have received, I do not think that cider can be produced in Canada from Canadian apples as cheaply as it can be produced in Somersetshire or any of the other apple growing counties in England. This industry
2336	COMMONS
Ways and Means-Customs Tariff
has been carried on in the old country for hundreds of years, it is part of their daily farm life. In spite of the degree of protection afforded this industry, it has never attained any considerable proportions in Canada. I can conceive of the Canadian cider industry being helped by the cultivation of an appetite for cider on the part of the Canadian people. The Canadian industry has not succeeded in bringing that about, but it is conceivable that the British cider people could do it with their wider advertising facilities. I am quite sure that the Canadian cider industry will not suffer as a result of this amendment, and it is quite possible that Canadians may become a little more partial to cider as a result of being able to obtain that article from Great Britain.
That is a very lame excuse.
Especially if it is hard cider.

British cider is to be allowed to come in free in order to help the Canadian industry; that is about the argument the minister is making. I wonder, if he used that argument in regard to all the other articles, where we would arrive. The apple industry in our district during the last few years has been labouring under a great depression. It has been difficult to find a market for other than No. 1 grade and a great deal of the other grades has gone into cider. The minister, by allowing British cider to come in free, is now trying to kill that little industry which we have been spending years in endeavouring to work up. We did have a protection of five to ten cents a gallon against British cider. The argument the minister advances is, to my mind, a very lame one and I wonder whether he would use it in regard to other articles as well.
What is the value of imports of cider from the United States?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
Last year we imported
$3 worth from the United States.
How much was exported from Canada?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: There is no export business from Canada.
Does the minister know how much cider is produced in Canada?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I have not the production figures. I might say for the information of my hon. friend, who, I am sure, wants to be fair-
Certainly.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: -that cider which contains more than 2i per cent of proof spirits would come in at duty of $2.50 per gallon from the old country.
That is not new cider.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
Many people think it is
better than the ordinary variety.
They keep that for home consumption.
The minister said that we had no exportations of cider.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
None, so far as I have
any record.

I should like to correct
that. My record shows that in 1929 we exported 6,327 gallons and in other years as much as 100,000 gallons.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
I thank my hon. friend
for the information.
Whereto?
If my hon. friend will take the trouble to look up the records, he can find that out.

speechtext: There is an increase. A considerable amount of evidence regarding this matter was placed before the tariff board. It linked itself up with the production of barley in Canada for malting purposes, the production of malt from that barley, the importation of malting barley from the United States for malting purposes and, finally, the importation of malt as such from the United States. I was astonished to find, for instance, that in 1929, in spite of the ability of this country to produce barley, we imported 41,000,000 pounds of malt from the United States.

At what value?

Ways and Means-Customs Tariff

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: $1,300,000. It will be noticed from what was done in committee yesterday that the rates of duty on barley were increased. This increase in the rate on malt follows that proportionately. I am sure of that.
Will that tend to increase British imports?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General

What was the former
duty on pulp made of rags?

speechtext:
That came under the
general provision for unclassified materials.

Is it increased under
this item?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
Of course, if it came
under this item, it would carry a duty of 25 per cent under the general tariff and per cent under the intermediate tariff. speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: Pulp has to be converted by grinding or by chemical process.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: That sounds a reasonable explanation.

My question was directed to the minister for this purpose. We have an insulating material made in this country out of refuse straw and wood pulp. The pulp material coming into this country carries a low rate of duty. On the American side they make this insulating material out of the refuse of the sugar cane, and what I was interested in was whether it would not be possible to have a duty on the finished article and still allow the manufacturers of insulating material in Canada to get their pulp in under this item.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: That is a matter of customs ruling, but I would point out to my hon. friend that even if the material he refers to were pulp it would still have to pay 25 per cent to come into this country.

If it was not
the intention to include the pulp of sugar cane in this item, could not the the difficulty be cleared up by adding the words " of a class or kind produced in Canada."

The very fact that the
minister is rather hazy on the question and admits it, and the rest of the house being just about as hazy, only emphasizes the danger of inserting an item as to which we do not know the whole facts. My hon. friend from Cariboo spoke of insulating material being made in Canada. There are in Canada at least one or two plants, and perhaps more, making insulating material. One of them that I know makes insulite. It is not made from wood pulp, but from the refuse, the bark, I take it, and other refuse from pulpwood. It is a very fine line of manufacture and is a
[Mr. Fraser.l
by-product of the pulp and paper industry. By a coincidence, I happened to receive a letter this morning from a very good friend of mine who is to-day in Finland. The pulp and paper production is quite important in Finland, and for market reasons or otherwise they desire to have a plant built for the manufacture of insulite out of the by-products of the pulp and paper industry. I happen to know that this same company is seriously considering building one of these plants in Canada. I just mention that in passing. I do not know positively whether this item would interfere with the establishment of such a plant in this country, but it is just possible it might have that effect because the by-products of the sugar cane, the sugar cane itself being brought in as pulp, might be used in the manufacture of insulating material.

If it came in under this

It might come in from,
the southern states, but would be more likely to come in from the British West Indies. I just mention that in passing as illustrative of the difficulty of settling these items intelligently in the house.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: Does the wording make it clear that the druggist who is imparting will get the benefit of this reduction?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: There is a point there as to the extent to which the druggist is using gelatin capsules in the manufacture of pharmaceutical preparations. What are the importations?

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext:
The hon. member for St. Boniface, who is a medical man, will be able to say whether or not the item as it now reads is wide enough to cover the druggist who uses these capsules in his business, and who might not be said to be in the manufacture of pharmaceutical preparations. As the item reads, it applies only to the manufacturer. The druggist is in a sense a manu-2419-1481
facturer when he fills the capsules on the prescription of the doctor, but in the other sense he is not a manufacturer. Whether this item as it is worded would enable the druggist to take advantage of it I cannot say.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition

speechtext: It is intended to apply to all who use these capsules by filling them.

speechtext: But one is a manufacturer, like a large firm, and the other is the country druggist.

speechtext: It is done by machinery in the one case, in a factory, and in the other case by the druggist on a doctor's prescription.
The druggist fills the capsules on the prescription of a doctor.

If this is intended to be of any advantage to the druggist, it is not well worded, because the druggist will often fill the capsules with something that has already been manufactured. He is simply filling the capsules, not manufacturing. The way the item is worded has the effect of making a donation to the man who is putting up a proprietary medicine.
Are these manufactured in Canada?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: No.

Is the minister
sure?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: The evidence before tin-tariff board was to that effect. I can orily rely on that.

That is one of the little things so very difficult to the business man. He has to give a certificate that these capsules are being used solely in the manufacture of medicinal and pharmaceutical preparations. This causes him the same trouble as I mentioned in regard to another article

these gelatine capsules are for use "exclusively in the manufacture of medicinal and pharmaceutical preparations." I do not know if the minister is familiar with them.

speechtext:
I have had to swallow
some.

speechtext:
The evidence given by

I understood one person
representing a gelatin works stated they had been figuring on making these capsules.

speechtext: And afterwards he wrote and said he was not interested. With regard to the important point raised first, I think, by the leader of the opposition, probably there might be some merit in inserting a word which at least would make it clear that the ordinary druggist who is filling these capsules would have the same right in connection with the matter as a large manufacturer.
Insert the words "or compounding."

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
"In the manufacture or
compounding" would cover everything, would it not?
Yes.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
The Minister of National Health (Mr. King) moves that the words "or compounding" be inserted after the word "manufacture." The item will then read:
Gelatin capsules, empty, when imported for use exclusively in the manufacture or compounding of medicinal or pharmaceutical preparation.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: This budget is another.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
My hon. friend will be
better satisfied with it by and by. We desire to do this with respect to the particular use to which gelatin capsules are put. Let us stick to that use instead of going into the unknown.

000.

in Canada.

That is the reason for

speechtext:
I cannot follow my
hon. friend's numbers. He is not quoting the item under discussion.

We are discussing 238a at
the present time, and we have just passed 237.

I have two manufacturers in my constituency manufacturing these goods. Some of the articles were not classified at all in any of the schedules. Mr. BENNETT And we are getting additional protection.

These several items are
luxuries and articles affected by questions of style. speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: About $22,000 worth.
It seems to me that there is too much protection in this case. The manufacturer is getting his moulds free, and then he has 15 per cent on the finished article.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: The previous item does not relate to this item at all. My hon. friend is comparing two items which are not related.

speechtext:
Blanks for lampshades
and combs might apply.

speechtext:
This enters to an untraceable extent, under item 711, which is the basket item of the whole tariff. The common name for this article is ethyl fluid, and it is a preparation the method of manufacture and the use of which in gasoline is covered by patents the world over. Up to the present the Canadian supply has come entirely from the United States, and has been imported by oil refiners in Canada who added the fluid to their gasoline products to produce a gasoline of low knock quality, the grade of which is continent wide and definitely set. Ethyl fluid can be added to any gasoline but ordinarily it is applied to the better refined gasolines. It has not been enumerated up to the present time in the tariff; that is, there has been no place for it at all, and it has been ruled dutiable under item 711. speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I desire
to bring to the attention of the minister a matter to which I think the government will be well advised to give its most serious consideration. I had hoped the hon. member for Medicine Hat (Mr. Gershaw) would be in his place for the discussion of this item. With very great effort there has been established near that city an industry, an earthenware industry, employing at times 110 hands. It has assets to the value of something more than $500,000 and has sold $320,000 worth of 6| per cent, twenty year bonds to investors throughout the province of Alberta. I fancy some of those bonds have been sold also in Saskatchewan and Manitoba. In other words, an effort has been made by the utilization of the resources of the country to establish a local industry.
That local industry has manufactured earthenware goods in very considerable quantities. Amongst other articles it has manufactured stone bottles in which Gurd's ginger beer is sold; and it has shown some signs of prosperity and at least has made progress. I need hardly say that with the limited local population the sales have not been very large; the entire sales of the concern last year did not reach $200,000. The little protection that it received enabled it not only to meet local requirements for jugs and earthenware of that kind, but to go further afield. I fancy

Ways and Means-Customs Tariff
there may be members of this house who have seen the products of this factory at western exhibitions, because the newspapers and public men and others throughout the west have been urging people to buy goods manufactured in Saskatchewan, manufactured in Alberta and manufactured in Manitoba, and while that campaign has been carried on the products of this plant have been shown at many of the small fairs and exhibitions throughout western Canada. Of course, to exist at all they have to do something more than merely local business, so they have pushed their trade east to meet the requirements of companies who use stone bottles, jugs and other similar articles. That has enabled them to maintain their plant, shall I say, to fair capacity and to give employment fairly regularly to about 110 people.
The competition of Glasgow manufacturers of just such commodities as are produced at this plant has been overcome by a duty of 15 per cent, which has just enabled them to keep the Canadian market along the lines I have indicated as against the competition from Great Britain. Now they are thoroughly alarmed. The gentlemen who placed the venture before the public are convinced that the result of this change will be ruinous to them. As far as they are concerned, while their loss will be insignificant, the injury to the small investor who has put up $500 or $1,000 in these 6j per cent, twenty-year bonds, will be very, very great.
The margin between success and failure is so small and the difficulties so enormous in the development of western industries that every help should be given to their development. Hon. gentlemen who remember the early days of commodities like Kitchener, will know of the struggle for existence which some industries had to experience before they reached a measure of strength which enabled them to compete with more powerful interests. In western Canada our struggles have been tremendous and the difficulties we have had to overcome have been very great. I have been in Calgary for thirty years, and I have seen the small manufacturing plants become important industries. Before this discussion ends, I intend to speak regarding another industry which employs 125 hands and which is placed in a very difficult position by one of the items in this tariff. The industry to which I am now referring is one which utilizes one of the natural resources of Canada-clay. They manufacture jugs, stone bottles and earthenware such as are mentioned here, and I still believe that it is better for 110 Canadians in Alberta to find employment in the manufacture of earthenware, than it is for 110 men in Great
Britain to find employment in the same industry. Such a condition is better for the British Empire, it is better for the Dominion of Canada, and certainly it is better for the province of Alberta. I urge the hon. minister as strongly as I can not to do anything which would jeopardize the interests of this little industry. Capital has been invested by men and women, in some cases from real desire to help their country. Those of you who have passed by Medicine Hat on the train have seen this little industry which is located I think both on the right and left side of the railway tracks. I have no personal interest in this matter, and so far as I can ascertain no immediate friends of mine are connected with it, but those who have made investments in these 6 j per cent twenty year bonds desire to see these clay beds utilized in the making of jugs and other products. When I attended a made-in-Alberta exhibition not long ago, I was surprised to see what they had been able to manufacture. I viewed with pardonable pride such a development in the industrial life of the west. It is true that at the present time it is only on a small scale, but they have been able to come down to Montreal and obtain business with the small protection they have at present. That protection enables them to compete successfully with the manufacturers in Scotland and Great Britain, but that protection is to be taken away.

speechtext:

That is the only reason for touching the item. I am not familiar with the feldspar situation. It probably would be wise to look into it. But at any rate my hon. friend will see that no change is being made with respect to it. That is, the situation after the budget is precisely the same as the situation was before, so far as it relates to feldspar. Perhaps he would be willing on the matter, because ground feldspar enters into many industries, and, as we often find in practice, one man's finished product is another man's raw material. I suggest to my hon. friend that if his case is as well founded, as I know he believes it is, it could be inquired into by the tariff board so that those who use this commodity would be able publicly to state what the effect would be of imposing a duty upon it.

I think the tariff board already has all the facts in relation to this matter. I might also refer to mica. How do the United States treat our mica? They admit free all our mica as ilt is taken out of the ground, but the minute we begin to treat it up goes their tariff. Consequently mica mining to-day in eastern Ontario is practically extinat. In the case of feldspar the tariff board has the facts, there is no great quantity involved, and I can assure the minister that if he does not take care of the industry it will meet the same fate as mica mining. There are some matters connected with the very decided increase in the duty under this item, as well as under other items, to which I should like to call attention. It has been constantly urged that the protection of these industries 'would mean the protection of the workmen engaged in them, but there is nothing whatever to show that such is the case. Generally speaking, a great many of the industries that are the most highfy protected pay the poorest wages. Industries in Canada which for years have been receiving from this government the advantage of special privileges are yet paying their workmen very poor wages indeed. In some connections other than that of the tariffs we have adopted the principle that the granting of concessions and special privileges, shall be dependent upon the maintenance of certain standards by the companies receiving the benefit of them. During the last few years, in awarding contracts-even in the granting of the charters-for the building of bridges, for example, we have insisted upon the inclusion of certain fair wage clauses. The proposal I should like to make is, that we ought not to grant any increase in the tariff until there is an understanding with the companies that they shall treat their employees fairly. We should insist on fair treatment for the men as to hours of employment, wages, and general conditions of labour, and that should be a condition precedent to the granting of any favours. Surely that is a fair proposal. It cannot be claimed to be very radical in its nature, although I would not hesitate to make it if it were. I am following a precedent that was recently set in the Ontario legislature. On February 12 last an application was made for an increase in the bounty on iron ore mined and smelted in Ontario. Though the application was granted, a protest was made in the legislature by a Liberal member, Mr. S. C. Tweed, president of the Ontario Equitable Life and Accident Insurance Company, who called attention to the fact that at the Algoma Steel works, at the Soo conditions of labour almost approaching slavery existed. He

Ways and Means-Customs Tariff
claimed that shifts of workingmen varied from eight to twelve hours for seven days in the week. Mr. Tweed's efforts were highly applauded by some of the leading papers in Ontario. I notice that the London Advertiser said:
The people of Ontario do not want an industry built on inordinate hours of labour. It would be too dear at such a price. Mr. Tweed performed a public service in directing attention to the conditions at the Soo. and any further grant of public money should be contingent upon safeguards for the workers. The assertion of the vice-president of the Algoma Steel Corporation that a change to the three-shift six-day system is being planned would be welcomed, and he will be held to his promise.
I would commend the statement in that editorial Let me repeat one phrase:
Any further grant of .public money should be contingent upon safeguards for the workers.
I should like to apply this principle to the matter before us, and insist that any further tariff concessions be made contingent upon safeguards for the workers. Commenting upon the Algoma situation, the Toronto Mail and Empire said:
These advances will cost the company an additional wage distribution of about $300,000 a year, but we believe that the change will be as profitable for the company in the long run as it should be beneficial to the employees so affected from the start. It is in harmony with the progressive spirit of the age.
It is difficult for the Algoma Steel Corporation at Sault Ste. Marie to bring about decent conditions of labour when its competitor at Sydney, the British Empire Steel Corporation, permits abominable conditions to exist. The minister speaks of implementing the report of the Duncan commission by granting extra aid to the steel industry. Let me say that there have been other commissions whose recommendations have not been implemented. I should like to refer to the commission appointed under order in council P.C. 1929, dated September 22, 1923, to inquire into conditions among the steel workers at Sydney, Nova Scotia. The report states:
To sum up: The fundamental causes of the recurring industrial unrest among the steel workers may be stated as follows:
(1)	The rate of wages.
(2)	The long hours of labour.

Labour agitators are condemned. May I quote from the report where the hours of labour are being dealt with:
A great deal of testimony was received to the effect that the men considered the hours of labour too long. In the department's in which the continuous process practice obtains, such as the blast furnaces, open hearth furnaces and coke ovens, the work is carried on on the two-shift plan. That requires the day-shift men to work eleven hours and the night-shift men thirteen hours. Once a fortnight when the men change shifts they work for a twenty-four hour change-over period.
A good deal of the work in connection with the continuous processes in the steel industry is quite intermittent in character. But when anything goes wrong the case is different and the twelve-hour day becomes a physical strain. The twelve-hour day with the seven-day week and the twenty-four hour change-over once a fortnight make a very exhausting combination.
A twelve-hour day followed steadily by any group of men for a considerable number of years means a decrease of their efficiency and a reduction of their vigour. The question of hours of labour has to be considered from a social as well as a physical point of view. A twelve-hour day in the plant means about thirteen hours away from his home and family for all the working days. That leaves little if any time for family life, recreation, social enjoyments and leisure.

I may say that the management apparently have no intention of improving the working conditions, even if they receive added tariff protection. Not very long ago I had a statement from some of the men there, and they pointed out that when they had approached Mr. Kelley with regard to this matter he had told them that although there was talk about the tariff, even if they received additional help it would be but a drop in the bucket. He referred as well to the bonus on coal used for the making of steel and this also he said had not materialized. The company were not in a position to give a general wage increase and had no intention whatever of doing so. If my correspondent rightly reports what has been said by his local manager it seems to me that we have a right at the present time to see that some pressure is brought to bear upon the company in this respect. As is shown by their statement, the company have been doing reasonably well; they have laid aside certain reserves. To go back to the statement of ministerial association, if it has been possible for them through good financing to lay aside certain reserves they ought to find it possible to make some provision for the men concerned. In the report two years ago of the ministerial association, the statement is made that #2,-000,000 had been retained for depreciation, or SI,000,000 per year, the balance presumably being available for interest charges on bonds and so on-
-while not a cent of this amount has been allowed for the better condition of the human element in the industry. It does cost money, doubtless a great deal, to replace the machinery of steel making. Unfortunately, it costs the industry little or nothing to replace men; there is nearly always a surplus of labour.

That is what they
like.

There is the condition which we face. Of course from the standpoint of the employer it is a good thing to have a surplus of labour, but surely we have reached the stage of civilization when a group of men such as hon. gentlemen here assembled in parliament, representing the people of Canada, ought to be in a position to insist upon our working men being enabled to live up to higher standards. The treaty of Versailles insisted upon the eight hour day, but we are told again and again by the government that under our constitution it is impossible to enforce the eight hour day in the provinces. Yet here is an opportunity for this government to insist upon it, and there is no reason why they should not do so. If they would stipulate that the increase in the tariff should be contingent upon a provision on the part of the industries concerned for the eight hour day, changes would be made in a very short time. A few years ago we were told we could not get the eight hour day in Canada because it did not prevail in the United States, and that therefore our people could not compete with the people in the United States. In at least the larger steel plants of the United States they have adopted the eight hour shift, yet we have not had such a move in the larger steel plants of Canada.
As I thought of this question I recalled an editorial which appeared in the Ottawa Journal of May 3, 1929, under the heading: Too Much of Paternalism. It was criticising the report of the industrial and international relations committee of this house; the particular report referred to endorsed the principle of unemployment insurance. The editorial is as follows:
It is perhaps fortunate for the country that neither this committee nor parliament possesses authority to give effect to the principle that is so lightly endorsed.
Further on it states:
It is to be hoped that parliament and the government find a resting place for these recommendations in the most convenient wastebasket. And the reason is clear. It is that if Canada keeps heeding all the reports that are made by committees, and goes on doing all the things that a lot of well-intentioned but misinformed people want her to do, then this country will become so burdened with paternalism and bureaucracy that the taxpayer will be crushed into the earth.
After conceding that some sort of unemployment insurance may be necessary in Great Britain, the editorial goes on to say:
But in Canada.sparsely settled, lacking in population, and passing through an era of tremendous development, the proposition that it is necessary to insure our people against unemployment is absurd.

The editorial concludes by deploring that we are " getting away from the old wholesome practice of individual effort." If the principles laid down by the Journal were applied to tariff privileges I wonder just what we would be doing. The steel companies and the protected industries in this country have been enjoying "paternalism" since confederation. We have been warned against the dole, but the industries have been receiving the dole with a vengeance, and in their case it has not been a small dole. If we are to insist upon individual effort on the part of workmen, why should we not insist upon the old wholesome practice of individual effort on the part of steel corporations? Why can these industries not stand on their own feet? The workers are expected to stand on their own feet, to work a twelve hour day and receive as wages mere miserable pittances. Some of the men working for these companies are receiving no more than 33 cents an hour. Yet the steel plants are permitting these very unwholesome conditions to continue. Of course it would be " paternalism " if we gave unemployment insurance; it would be "paternalism" if we prevented the men from working seven days in the week and from working eleven and thirteen hour shifts.
There is an opportunity for this government to do the just thing by a large body of workers. Within two months the elections will be at hand, and from the Atlantic to the Pacific the Liberals and Conservatives will be appealing to the factory workers to support them. The Liberals will take the ground that in some way or another this budget is protecting their interests. The Conservatives will say that if they are elected they will make it their business to protect the workman. Here is the chance for both parties. If the Conservatives are in earnest and insist upon it, I think they can force the government to give the workers the conditions they deserve. On the other hand, if the government is in earnest in its profession of a real desire to put the eight hour day in operation, and has been barred from doing so only by constitutional difficulties, this affords it an admirable opportunity for action. There are a certain number of hon. members on both sides of the house who wish well to their fellow men and it is for them to insist that this intolerable condition no longer obtains.

Mr. Chairman, I wish to congratulate my hon. friend from Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Woodsworth) upon his very eloquent address. It is always a pleasure to me to listen to him and to-night he has ably championed the case of the working men

in the steel industry. This government, by the enactment of Bill No. 49, has shown its good will towards the workers. This bill has to do with the eight hour day and fair wages in government contracts or in work performed for the Dominion government. During this session I had the opportunity to point out that the provinces have full jurisdiction with regard to the eight hour day and fair wages, and I wonder that the provinces have not followed the example of British Columbia, which has adopted minimum wage laws for men and women.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: So has Alberta.

If my hon. friend will
permit, there is only one wage law in the province of Alberta respecting minimum wages. That relates to women, and it contains a provision also to the effect that the wages of men shall not be lower than the wages of women, but that does not mean much, as my hon. friend knows. The hon. gentleman is a most distinguished lawyer and is very well acquainted with the fact that in his own province there is no distinct law relating to minimum wages for men and it is exactly the same in Ontario. So I believe I am fair in saying that there is only one minimum wage law for men, and that is in British Columbia. In the other provinces what has been done for the men does not amount to so much, because if the men who work in the steel plants are not paid more than young girls who work in laundries, I do not believe it is fair. At all events, except on Dominion government contracts, the wages to be paid and hours to be worked is a matter for the provincial governments to deal with. Some of the governments have already taken steps with regard to the hours of labour and the wages paid on their own provincial works, but that is not sufficient. The federal government, outside of works under its own control, has no jurisdiction to enact legislation in respect to fair wages or the eight hour day or the forty-four hour week; so I do not understand why the provinces do not take steps to give the working men a chance, by passing laws to the effect that working men should not work more than forty-four hours a week and should receive a decent salary. I believe, Mr. Chairman, that this would be fair; and when I speak of the matter in this house it is because what is said here is recorded in Hansard and is read throughout the country. It is a matter of momentous importance to thousands upon thousands of people. I do not understand how a mother could bring up and look after a family on a wage of $2 or

$2.50 a day, which she receives from her husband every two weeks. The industries which make a fair profit should share that profit with their co-workers, and we have examples of that being done. We have the example of Mr. Ford, who pays very high wages and who is one of the richest men in the United States. He is not stingy in dealing with his working men; he considers them rather as partners, and experience has shown that he has not suffered from that policy- far from it.	[DOT]
In summing up, I do not see how the federal government could try to hold up these concerns; if they did so the companies would say that they had no chance to pay fair wages. But I believe the provincial governments which are interested in the matter should make a study of the situation and be bold enough to take a step which will be a benefit to all concerned. Merchants, doctors and every one will benefit if the working men are paid better wages; they will have more money to spend; they will live more comfortably, and the governments will then have less to spend in the way of relief and for public health. I believe this matter is entirely under the jurisdiction of the provincial governments, and they should look after it at the earliest possible opportunity.

Mr. Chairman, I
wish very strongly and emphatically to associate myself with the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre in the very excellent case which he has made for some consideration on the part of this government for the steel workers in Sydney. It is true that the budget offers something to the British Empiie Steel Corporation. I am not here to hold any brief for that corporation; I should like to see it get fair play, but I am particularly anxious that it should give fair play to those people out of whose sweat and blood the corporation's profits are made. No member of this house, if he is fair, whether he is a Liberal a Conservative, a Progressive or a Labour man, can argue that the British Empire Steel Corporation is doing what is right and fair when it compels its men ^ to work thirteen hours a day, as they are doing in some cases, and ten hours a day as they are doing in all cases. A great many of these men do not even get one day off a week; they are compelled to work on Sunday as well.
In this budget the government has offered certain financial concessions, both by bonus and by direct protection, to the British Empire Steel Corporation. For my part I consider that the British Empire Steel Corporation is well able to take care of itself,
but the men who are employed by that corporation are not able to take care of themselves, as has been shown by the unfortunate experiences these men have had in the years during which they have been employees of that corporation. Before these items pass and before these concessions are given to the British Empire Steel Corporation I believe all parties in this house, irrespective of political affiliations, should join together and say that for once in this country we are going to place human values ahead of any other values that may be considered later. For my part I would not want one single concession made to the British Empire Steel Corporation by this government unless the government first bargained with them to give their employees a fair deal in the matter of wages and working hours.
When those of U3 who are interested in a shorter working day and better wages for labour in this country speak in parliament, we are immediately confronted with the British North America Act. Hon. gentlemen say, "Oh, the constitution will not allow us to do this." Here is a case where a corporation is looking for your money, for the money of the taxpayers of Canada and for the money of .the steel workers of Sydney. Before that money is turned over to them this government has a golden opportunity to get away from the constitutional objection and say to that corporation-which I suppose, like other corporations, will do almost anything for money-"Give your workingmen the eight-hour day and we will give you the concessions promised in our budget." Unless the workingmen of Sydney get some benefit from these concessions, I am opposed to them; for any company which compels its workmen in this civilized and Christian age to work twelve hours a day and a great many of them to work seven days a week, should not be given any concessions by a civilized government. That is the stand I take, and I do not care who likes it or who does not like it. I think the Minister of Finance should hold up these portions of his budget, get in touch with the heads of that corporation and say, "We are willing to do this for you provided you are prepared to deal fairly with the men whom you employ." An opportunity is thus offered to get away from the constitutional objection, and all parities in the house can unite to do something for those men who have been so unfairly treated for many years.

Mr. Chairman, I have to agree with a great deal of what has been said by the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Woods-worth). I think I can say that I know more
