I know something about the hours of labour and about their living conditions, and I supported this budget because it contained a clause which might be of some help to those men. The hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre has delivered this same type of speech for many years, but those speeches always have been futile because they never had any practical object in view. I have a practical object in view, and when the resolution comes before this house I am going to move that a provision be added that the money be not paid to the steel company unless it shall find its way into the wage envelopes of the men. That is a practical suggestion worth more to these men than all the speeches which the hon. member could deliver during the next ten years.
This thing has to be considered from a common sense point of view. If the steel company at Sydney can afford to pay higher wages and operate on an eight hour day, it should be compelled to do so. If, on the other hand, it cannot afford to operate under those conditions, then no law which we pass in this house is going to compel it to do .so. How are we going to find out the true state of affairs? There is a Labour department in this country whose duty it is to have found out these things long ago. If that department were properly organized and properly functioning it would have known of the financial condition of the Dominion Iron & Steel Company, and would have known whether that company was able to pay increased wages. The department has fair wage officers and experts who could have obtained this information. No assistance was given to me when I took the stand I did upon the budget. It cost me something to do that, but while I remain in this house I propose always to have some practical object in view whenever I speak either on behalf of the labouring man or upon any other subject. I do not propose to take up the time of the committee in making futile observations regarding the conditions which obtain down there. We have heard the reports of the ministerial association-we had Rev. Doctor C. W. Gordon down there last year-and everything they say is true. The conditions under which the men work are not satisfactory and are such as no honest Canadian citizen should have to put up with. If that concern can afford to pay higher wages we should see that it does so. There is only one way we can do that, and that is the course I propose to adopt. At that time we will find out just where these gentlemen stand.

Mr. Chairman, for several
sessions the house has been discussing the question of higher wages for employees of the government, and from all parts of the house we have had expressions of opinion in favour of granting to them a higher wage. That expression of opinion was not confined to any particular party, and I hope, now that this question has come up of providing better working conditions and higher pay for those employed by the steel companies, it will re-seive the same unanimous support.
For a number of years we have listened in this house to the pleas of hon. members from the maritime provinces regarding maritime rights. There is hardly a member from that part of the country who has not risen in his place and said that he was in some way or the other a maritime-rigbter. If ever there was a time when the members from the maritimes should be fighting for maritime rights, this is it. It is a fine thing to fight for protection for industry, it may be a fine thing to fight for protection for capital, which is really protection for industry, but it is much more important to fight for protection for the human beings who are employed in such industries. We are fighting to-night for protection for those human beings who create dividends for the share and bond holders of these various corporations, and I hope the Liberal members will not be more backward than some of the Conservative members have been. I am sure it would be a reflection upon the Liberal party if they permitted the Conservative party to stand alone in a fight for better living conditions for those who make millions of dollars for the shareholders of these corporations. We find that already the value of the shares of the steel companies has risen, no doubt as a result of the budget introduced by the hon. Minister of Finance.

Mr. R. L. Calder, a lawyer, who is probably well known to hon. members, speaking only recently on the question of conditions in Nova Scotia, made the statement that it was "like a suburb in hell" which the people were compelled to live in. Industrial scientists in Great Britain have stated, after very exhaustive inquiry and experiment, that the maximum efficiency of the human machine is realized on a working week of forty hours.

It is strange what a change has come over hon. gentlemen opposite in the last few years. One of the reasons for the unemployment that has existed in Canada during the last eight years since this government has been in power is the withering condition of the coal and iron and steel industries. When I came into this house in the session of 1922 I introduced a resolution, which I reintroduced in 1923 and in 1924, asking for bonuses and subventions and subsidies and protection along the line of Mr. Baldwin's policy in the old country for these three great industries. The coal industry, the steel industry, and the iron industry are key industries in Canada, and upon their success depends the success of agriculture and all the other industries in this country. In the session of 1922, and again in 1923 and 1924, long before the present Minister of Finance was in this house, when he was away up in Saskatchewan sitting as a member of a provincial cabinet, this government voted down the motion of a private member for a national coal supply. That motion was introduced for the purpose of seeing that every ton of coal used in this country was produced under the British flag -in England and Wales, in Alberta and the maritimes. I also asked for an embargo against the $56,000,000 which this country sends down annually to the Pennsylvania coal barons. That amount would have provided a very large sum for these key industries in the maritime provinces in the way of bonuses, subventions and subsidies. Where was the government of the day then? It was hanging on to office by a majority of one or two or three, and it voted down this resolution in 1922, 1923 and 1924.
So far as the Duncan commission is concerned, its appointment was forced upon the
government by the Conservative opposition in this house. Debates took place in the house from 1922 to 1926 exposing conditions in the maritime provinces, as a result of which the government was forced to appoint the Duncan commission. So I do not think the country will be very well pleased with the attitude of hon. gentlemen opposite fh this connection, because if there is one agency that has contributed to unemployment in Canada, especially in the maritimes, more than anything else it has been the withering condition of the iron and coal and steel industries. The government did nothing during all the years it was in power to better the condition of those industries. The employees in those three industries were allowed to starve to death, and the industries themselves to wither. But now the government come along and climb on the protection band wagon.
I wonder if the Minister of Finance has any amendments to make to these tariff schedules. Is there an additional budget to be brought in regarding steel and coal and iron, as there was regarding fruits and vegetables? Are we to have a sort of second budget for these industries as we had for fruits and vegetables?
I say, Mr. Chairman, that if credit is due for forcing the government to adopt the protective system, and the safeguarding of our key industries, it is due to the Conservative opposition in this house. The government did not care anything at all about these industries so long as they could grab a few free trade votes and hang on to office. The industries were allowed to wither away and the employees and their families to starve to death for want of work. speakerposition: Chief Government Whip
speechtext:
The statement which Mr. Tweed made, and which my hon. friend repeated on the floor of this house, are entirely foreign to the facts. I have lived in the city of Sault Ste Marie for thirty years and am more or less familiar with the conditions under which the men who work in that steel industry live. Those conditions are not in every respect ideal. But one of the best evidences that they have not been as bad as my hon. friend's quotation would lead us to believe is the fact that the most friendly relations have prevailed between the men and the management of the company. There have been no labour troubles for the last twenty-five years in that steel industry at Sault Ste Marie. It is true that many of the men have to work from eleven to thirteen hours a day. That is too long, and I am in entire agreement with what my hon. friend had to say in that respect. I am in favour of the eight hour day. But here were the conditions. The steel industry was able to operate only during a portion of the year owing to the fact that the large steel industries of the United States were dumping their products over here at a price with which the local industry could not compete. Had this industry several years ago been given the protection that they should have had in order to afford them a fair chance in their own market, then I am satisfied the management of the steel company at the Soo would have given the men
[Mr. Church.)
the eight hour day long before this; and it would have been protection for the men as v/ell as for the industry. As a matter of fact I know that the management of the Algonna Steel Corporation have been working on the scheme of an eight hour day, and just as soon as they can afford to put it into operation they will do so. The provisions contained in the budget with respect to steel will help in that regard. Whether or not they go far enough to enable the steel companies to do that has yet to be proven. I hope they will, and that as a result the men will be placed on the eight hour shift in the very near future. But there is this feature to be remembered in connection with the eight hour day. The great majority of the men who are working the longer hours are working on a tonnage basis, and the longer they work the more they earn. Some of those men-I do not think this applies to all of them-have told me that when the mills were operating only a portion of the year they were anxious to work the longer hours and make more money while they had the opportunity. But the ideal condition is to enable the steel industry to have a fair show in their own market that they may supply the steel requirements of that market, and when they get that they will be able to deal more fairly with their men in regard to working hours and working conditions than they have been able to do in the past.

The men at the Algoma mills are not organized. I happened to be with the British parliamentatry delegation that visited this country two years ago. When we were passing through the Sault in connection with the trip eastward, a deputation waited upon Mr. Tom Johnston, Mr. Tom Shaw and other Labour members of that delegation. I might

say that the British delegates were absolutely appalled at the conditions revealed by the deputation that appeared. There was no organization whatever and the men were absolutely afraid to make independent representations. The governor in council may, by order in council, direct that there be substituted for tariff item 388 in schedule A of the Customs Tariff, 1907, and the several rates of duties of customs set opposite said item in schedule A the following:
Iron or steel angles, beams, channels, columns, girders, joists, piling, tees, zees, and other shapes or sections, not punched, drilled or further manufactured than hot rolled, weighing not less than one hundred and twenty pounds per lineal yard, n.o.p., per ton: British preferential tariff, $2; intermediate tariff, $2; general tariff, $3.
From and after the publication of such order in council in the Canada Gazette, tariff item 388 as it appeal's in said schedule at the time of passing of this act, shall be repealed and the provisions of the said tariff item as it appears in the last preceding subsection of this section shall be substituted therefor.
The governor in council shall not direct that such provisions shall be substituted as aforesaid unless and until the Governor in Council is satisfied that iron or steel angles, beams, channels, columns, girders, joists, piling, tees, zees, and other shapes or sections weighing less than one hundred and twenty pounds per lineal yard are manufactured in substantial quantities in Canada from steel made in Canada.

I know there is no use in making any objection to these items, but I am advised that this change under item 388b will ruin some of the plants engaged in fabricating iron and steel. One plant in my own city advises me

that this means absolute ruin. I suppose it is of no avail to protest, but I feel it is my duty to direct the attention of the minister and of the government to this situation.

I want to protest once more. We have item 388 with a duty of SI per ton, which is less than the duty on the pig iron from which these articles are produced. Is there anything more ridiculous in the tariff? The whole tariff is ridiculous and will be absolutely useless as far as protecting the iron and steel industry is concerned. I venture to say that twelve months from now the minister will be forced to agree with what I am saying.
He wifi not be here.
I hope he will be in the house so that I may have the satisfaction of showing him how this has worked out in one year.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: My hon. friend may not be here himself.
Perhaps not, but in that case I can write the minister a letter.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: There is a matter here to which I directed attention some time ago. Power is given to change the tariff by executive action, and notice is to be given in the Canada Gazette, but the new tariff is to be operative forthwith. As I have said on previous occasions in dealing with other matters, I think notice of fifteen or thirty days should be given, as the case may be. It is rather unfair to provide that a new tariff may be promulgated by executive action without affording at least some opportunity of knowledge to those who may be concerned.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I should point out to my hon. friend that this item is exactly the same as it has stood in the tariff since 1914. However, I will bear in mind what he has said.
